promptText: What is the central mental model the chapter proposes for thinking about a vector index in enterprise RAG?
options: A materialized, permissioned view over many source systems that must inherit both the freshness and access-control obligations of every system it draws from
A stateless cache that can be safely rebuilt from scratch at any time with no security implications
A one-time snapshot that never needs to be refreshed once built
A replacement for the source systems, making the originals unnecessary
explanation: Like a relational materialized view, the vector index is a precomputed copy that must not silently bypass the base systems' row-level security or freshness obligations just because it is a separate physical copy.

promptText: Why is it insufficient to enforce access control only by instructing the model in the prompt to 'only answer using documents the user is authorized to see'?
options: Prompts cannot contain the word 'authorized'

The model has no tamper-proof way to distinguish authorized from unauthorized content, and if unauthorized content was already retrieved into the context, it has already crossed a security boundary regardless of what the model does with it
Prompt-based instructions always increase latency by 10x
This approach works fine and is the industry-standard method
explanation: Authorization must be enforced as a hard filter on what content can ever be returned by retrieval, not as an instruction hoping the model self-polices — a direct consequence of prompt injection risk.

promptText: Why must permission filtering happen as a pre-filter inside the vector search rather than as a post-filter on the results?
options: Post-filtering is always slower to compute, regardless of any security concerns

Post-filtering both degrades answer quality (few or weak results survive) and is a security anti-pattern, since unauthorized content may already have touched logging, caching, or downstream systems before the post-filter runs
Vector databases physically cannot support post-filtering
Pre-filtering is required only for public, non-sensitive content
explanation: If most top-K semantically similar chunks belong to unauthorized documents, post-filtering can leave too few good results, and any intermediate system (LLM call, cache, logs) that touched the unauthorized content before filtering has already leaked it.

promptText: What is the recommended way to handle deletion or access-revocation events from a source system?
options: Ignore them until the next scheduled full re-crawl, since deletions are rare
Propagate them through the same CDC/connector mechanism as content edits, with high priority, since a stale permission is a live security exposure, not just a stale fact
Handle deletions only manually, once per year, during an audit
Deletions cannot be propagated to a vector index at all
explanation: The chapter treats access revocation as a higher-priority event class than routine content updates, because a stale permission is a security incident while a stale fact is merely an inconvenience.

promptText: Why does generative synthesis in RAG create a strictly harder security problem than classic enterprise search's ranked list of ten links?
options: Generative synthesis requires ten times more storage than a ranked list

A ranked list of links is self-limiting exposure (a user sees only a title), whereas generation compresses many chunks into one fluent answer, so a single leaked chunk can silently shape the final answer even if the user never sees the source
Enterprise search never had any access control at all
Generation always runs on a separate, unmonitored server
explanation: A ranked list showing an unauthorized document's title is a smaller leak than a system that reads that document's full contents and confidently answers using it — synthesis hides the provenance of a leaked fact inside a fluent answer.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend NOT making a live, synchronous call back to Confluence/SharePoint to check permissions on every single retrieval query?
options: Because source systems' APIs are always down

Because it would add unacceptable latency and load to source systems never designed to be queried per-token-generation; instead, permission state should be denormalized into the index at ingestion time and kept current via the same CDC stream as content
Because live permission checks are illegal under GDPR
Because vector databases cannot make outbound HTTP calls
explanation: The production architecture explicitly avoids a live round-trip to source systems per query; ACLs are captured and kept fresh in the index itself, treating access revocation as the same kind of event as a content edit.

promptText: How does a restrictive permission filter interact with ANN (approximate nearest neighbor) recall, and why does this matter for enterprise deployments?
options: ANN indexes are unaffected by any metadata filter under any circumstances

ANN indexes are tuned assuming the candidate pool roughly matches the true top-K; applying a restrictive filter as a post-filter on an already-approximate search can yield far fewer than K usable results or degraded relevance, since the index never specifically searched within that narrow subset
Restrictive filters always improve ANN recall by reducing the search space
This interaction only matters for exact (brute-force) search, never for ANN
explanation: This is why modern vector databases increasingly support filtered ANN search (predicate incorporated during graph traversal) so recall quality is preserved even for narrow, highly-restricted user permission sets.

promptText: Why does the chapter state that ingestion throughput requirements scale with corpus churn, not corpus size?
options: Because larger corpora always have proportionally lower churn rates

Because a corpus that is mostly static needs a very different pipeline and budget than one with the same size but high daily churn, since keeping current requires sustained re-embedding/re-indexing throughput proportional to the rate of change, not the total document count
Because corpus size has no effect on any part of the ingestion pipeline
Because churn only matters for the query pipeline, never for ingestion
explanation: A 2-million-document corpus with 5% daily churn requires sustained throughput of roughly 100,000 documents/day to stay current — a capacity-planning number driven by churn rate, not total corpus size.

promptText: How should a chunk with mixed public and restricted content (e.g., field-level permissions within one record) be handled during chunking?
options: Fixed-size chunking should always be used regardless of permission boundaries, since ACLs can be patched in at query time

The document should be chunked along the same boundaries as the permission boundaries, splitting restricted fields into their own chunks with tighter ACLs, even if this means less 'natural' chunk boundaries
Mixed-permission documents should never be ingested into any RAG system
The entire document should be marked public if any part of it is public
explanation: A single chunk straddling a public and a restricted field cannot have one correct ACL attached; security requirements here directly override what would otherwise be the ideal chunking strategy from a pure retrieval-quality standpoint.

promptText: Why is keying chunks by a content hash alone (rather than a stable document-ID + position key) a common ingestion mistake?
options: Content hashes are always slower to compute than embeddings
Every edit produces an entirely new key since the hash changes, leaving the old, now-stale chunk silently orphaned in the index forever instead of being replaced
Content hashes cannot be stored as vector metadata
Content-hash keys are incompatible with all vector databases
explanation: A stable key derived from source document ID plus a stable position identifier allows re-ingestion to upsert/overwrite the same logical chunk; a content-hash key changes on every edit and leaves stale duplicates behind.

promptText: Why is 'last-modified timestamp' from the source system not sufficient on its own to guarantee freshness in a distributed ingestion pipeline?
options: Timestamps are always stored in the wrong timezone

It tells you when the source changed but nothing about whether the pipeline actually processed that change successfully — a connector can fail silently on one document while the source's timestamp keeps advancing on subsequent edits, masking a stuck document
Timestamps cannot be compared across different source systems under any circumstances
Freshness should only ever be measured in the source system, never in the index
explanation: Real freshness monitoring needs 'time since this document was last successfully re-indexed' per document, reconciled against source history, not just the source's raw last-modified value, which a naive dashboard would misleadingly show as fine.

promptText: A bank's compliance review asks 'can you prove a specific user could never have retrieved a specific document?' Which architectural combination best preempts this objection?
options: A post-filtering step plus verbal assurance from engineering that the model 'usually' respects permissions

Pre-filtered, ACL-pushed-down retrieval architecture plus a reproducible, immutable audit trail that logs the resolved filter predicate and retrieved chunk IDs for every query, enabling reconstruction of exactly what could have been retrieved for any historical query
Encrypting the entire vector index at rest with no metadata filtering
Running the RAG system only during business hours to limit exposure
explanation: The chapter stresses that pre-filtering plus a full audit log of resolved predicates and retrieved chunk IDs (not just cited ones) lets a team reconstruct 'why did the assistant say X' and demonstrate structural exclusion, which is what compliance reviews actually demand.

promptText: Why does the chapter caution against a 'fail open' default when a source-system connector or ACL evaluation temporarily errors out during ingestion or query time?
options: Fail-open behavior is always faster and therefore preferred for latency-critical paths

A transient error causing the query to proceed unfiltered or with an overly permissive default would silently turn an infrastructure hiccup into a data breach; the correct design fails closed, returning an error rather than an unfiltered result set
Fail-open only matters for ingestion pipelines, never for query-time permission resolution
There is no meaningful difference between fail-open and fail-closed for RAG systems
explanation: This mirrors general security engineering principle: when the security-relevant portion of a predicate cannot be resolved with confidence, the system must refuse rather than silently degrade to an unfiltered or overly-permissive query.

promptText: For a database-table connector, why does its 'ACL' typically need translation before it fits the platform's common ACL schema, unlike a Confluence or SharePoint connector?
options: Databases never have any access control concept at all

Database ACLs are often expressed as row-level security predicates or role grants (SQL-level constructs) rather than a document-level permission list, so they must be translated into the same normalized ACL metadata format used across all connectors — a common source of under- or over-restriction bugs if done naively
Database connectors are always exempt from ACL requirements
SQL databases automatically export their ACLs in the platform's native format with zero translation needed
explanation: The chapter specifically flags database sources as a case where 'ACL' may need per-user, query-time evaluation rather than purely denormalized capture, since row-level security predicates don't map cleanly onto a flat group-based document ACL schema.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend centralizing ingestion (connectors, ACL propagation, freshness) across a shared enterprise RAG platform while federating some retrieval-time decisions (top-K, reranking aggressiveness) to individual product teams?
options: Because ingestion has no security implications, unlike retrieval

Because the hard, security-sensitive engineering in ingestion is the same regardless of consuming team and is far better fixed once centrally, whereas the right precision/recall trade-off in retrieval genuinely differs per use case, so federating that layer preserves flexibility without duplicating risky infrastructure
Because federating ingestion is technically impossible with any vector database
Because retrieval-time decisions must always be identical across all teams for consistency
explanation: Centralizing the riskier, reusable engineering (ACLs, connectors, freshness) avoids each team independently getting security wrong in different ways, while federating retrieval-tuning choices lets each product's needs (e.g., compliance lookup vs. casual FAQ bot) diverge appropriately.
